walkthroughs.body_html:
Sociology Basics: Key Concepts & Processes — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Sociology Basics: Key Concepts & Processes brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Sociology Basics: Key Concepts & Processes.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Murdock (1949) identified how many family functions?

options: Ethnocentrism means concentrating on your own ethnic group only.
Ethnocentrism is the same as racism.

Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own — assuming one's own cultural practices and values are normal or superior. It is a methodological problem in social research as well as a social phenomenon.
Schools teach pupils to correspond with each other through letters.
School subjects must match employer demands.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.
School structures mirror workplace structures, preparing pupils for capitalist labour.

mcqs.q: Why do positivists and interpretivists prefer different methods?
options: Positivists like numbers and interpretivists like words — that's the whole difference.

Positivists treat sociology like natural science, seeking objective measurable patterns — preferring quantitative methods. Interpretivists believe humans construct meaning, requiring qualitative methods to access subjective experience.
Ethnocentrism means concentrating on your own ethnic group only.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.
